title: Predictive wavelength tailoring of uniform GaSb-based quantum dots for emission at 1.55 um
authors: Markus Peil, Maja Wasiluk, Ziemowit Olinkiewicz, Tymon Przychodni, Robert Matysiak, Teemu Taskinen, Joona Salonen, Abhiroop Chellu, Metin Patli, Joonas Hilska, Anna Musiał, Michał Gawełczyk, Mircea Guina, Teemu Hakkarainen
abstract: A detailed study of emission wavelength tailoring of GaSb-based QDs formed by InGaSb-filling of droplet-etched nanoholes in AlGaSb is presented. The study shows that the emission wavelength can be modified from 1.48 um to the center of the telecom C-band at 1.55 mm by independently varying the QD composition and size. More specifically, the optical transition energy shifts linearly as a function of In-content of the QD material at a rate of -4.4 meV/In-percentage, and with the number of monolayers (ML) of material used for filling the nanoholes, at -2.0 meV/ML. These experimentally observed energy shifts are well predicted by simulations yielding rates of -4.3 meV/In-percentage and -2.1 meV/ML, respectively. For the simulation, a uniform In composition, low intermixing, and microscopically measured QD geometry is considered. Additionally, excellent ensemble QD uniformity, with unprecedented inhomogeneous broadening well-below 7 meV across all samples is demonstrated. Finally, photoluminescence of single-QDs reveals narrow excitonic emission lines of 13.8+/-6.7 ueV and low fine-structure splitting values reaching <10 ueV. These results identify GaSb-based LDE QDs as a tunable telecom platform for scaling quantum-photonic applications over long-haul optical fiber networks.
summary: This paper reports on the development of GaSb-based quantum dots as a highly promising platform for quantum photonics. By combining experimental measurements and advanced simulations, the authors demonstrate precise, predictable tuning of the emission wavelength across the entire telecom C-band. This work establishes a robust, scalable source for single photons essential for quantum communication technologies.
main_problem: The goal is to create a highly tunable, solid-state quantum light source capable of emitting single photons at the telecom C-band (1.55 $\mu$m) for long-haul quantum communication networks.
main_result: The study successfully demonstrated that the emission wavelength can be tuned from 1.48 $\mu$m to 1.55 $\mu$m by independently controlling the quantum dot composition (In-content) and size (monolayers).
method: The research combines experimental photoluminescence measurements with detailed theoretical simulations using multiband k.p theory to predict and explain the optical transition energy shifts.
model_or_system: The physical platform consists of GaSb-based quantum dots formed via InGaSb-filling of nanoholes etched into AlGaSb layers. The electronic structure is modeled using envelope function approximations incorporating strain and Coulomb interactions.
key_observables: Emission wavelength (tunable from 1.48 $\mu$m to 1.55 $\mu$m), inhomogeneous broadening (< 7 meV), narrow single-QD excitonic linewidth ($\sim 13.8 \mu	ext{eV}$), and the linear energy shift rates ($	ext{-4.4 meV}/	ext{In}\%$, $	ext{-2.0 meV}/	ext{ML}$).
important_parameters: In-content percentage ($x$), number of monolayers (ML), and the target telecom wavelength of 1.55 $\mu$m.
main_assumptions: Simulations assume uniform In composition, low intermixing, and utilize microscopically measured QD geometries; the observed uniformity is assumed to be limited by the initial nanohole population.
figures_summary: The notes suggest figures illustrate the QD structure (AFM/SEM), cross-sections showing strain, and PL spectra showing the tunable redshift of the exciton energy versus In-content.
paper_structure: The paper follows a structure of presenting the physical system and fabrication process, detailing the experimental measurements (PL spectroscopy), presenting the theoretical framework (k.p modeling), and finally quantifying the tunability and uniformity of the resulting quantum emitters.
why_interesting: This work directly addresses the hardware requirements for quantum networks by providing a solid-state, tunable, and high-quality single-photon source operating at the critical telecom wavelength.
